title: A Reluctant Rise In EV Prices
gist: This is a short teaser/abstract (the full report is paywalled): China's roughly three-year EV price war has paused, with average EV prices rising back to mid-2024 levels, but Gavekal's Ernan Cui argues this reflects rising costs rather than reduced competition, so producer profits aren't actually improving even as the pricing relief risks further denting already-softening EV demand.

themes.theme: China's EV price war pauses, but for the wrong reason

insights.claim: After nearly three years of steady price declines, all major Chinese EV automakers raised prices in the months leading up to August 2026.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: A multi-year deflationary price war in China's EV sector appears to be pausing, which could ease margin pressure across the value chain if it persists.
insights.quote: After nearly three years of steady declines in prices, all major automakers have raised prices in recent months.
insights.locator: Is China's legendary price war in electric vehicles finally over?

insights.claim: The average price of EVs sold in China in August 2026 was around RMB178,000, up from around RMB168,000 a year earlier and roughly back to mid-2024 levels.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Concrete price levels to track: a ~6% YoY rise erases roughly a year and a half of price declines, a useful benchmark for monitoring whether the trend continues.
insights.quote: The average price of EVs sold in August was around RMB178,000, up from around RMB168,000 a year ago and roughly back to where it was in the middle of 2024.
insights.locator: The average price of EVs sold in August was around RMB178,000

insights.claim: Rising EV prices in China are being driven by higher production costs rather than by reduced competition among automakers, so they are not translating into more sustainable profits for EV makers even though this is superficially what Beijing's crackdown on 'involutionary' competition was meant to achieve.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Don't read higher EV prices as a margin-recovery signal for Chinese automakers; the profitability thesis behind the price-war-ending narrative looks weaker than it appears on the surface.
insights.quote: today's higher prices are not translating into more sustainable profits for EV makers, because they are the result of higher costs rather than reduced competition
insights.locator: On the surface, that's exactly what the government has been trying to achieve

insights.claim: Higher EV prices in China risk becoming a further headwind for vehicle sales at a time when households are already cutting back on EV purchases.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Watch Chinese EV volume data for confirmation; a demand slowdown compounded by price increases could pressure both automaker revenues and the broader battery/supply-chain ecosystem.
insights.quote: higher prices risk turning into another headwind for sales at a time when households are already reducing purchases of EVs
insights.locator: More worryingly, higher prices risk turning into another headwind

insights.claim: China's EV price war began in early 2023 when Tesla and BYD cut prices sharply to capture market share amid the post-Covid reopening, prompting other automakers to follow; falling battery prices and production-technology gains sustained years of intense feature-for-price competition that squeezed producer margins without triggering industry consolidation.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Explains the mechanism behind the price war's persistence: cheap batteries and tech gains let weak-margin players keep competing rather than exit, so any resumption of cost deflation could restart price cuts without the shakeout investors might expect.
insights.quote: The falling prices squeezed margins for producers but did not trigger significant consolidation in the industry.
insights.locator: EV prices started falling in early 2023, when market leaders Tesla and BYD
